Geospatial data

Source: vignettes/geospatial.Rmd
geospatial.Rmd

rcs stores sf objects and terra rasters next to tables, in the same store and with the same functions. This vignette shows what the package adds to geospatial data when it writes them, and how to read only the rows that intersect an area. It assumes you have read vignette("rcs").

Geocoding needs the package h3o, and rasters need terra. Both are suggested, not required; the code below that uses them runs only when they are installed.

library(rcs)
library(sf)
st <- store_connect(file.path(tempdir(), "geo-store"), create = TRUE)

Write an sf object

rcs_sim_polygons() returns simulated polygons in a box of open ocean, between longitudes −30 and −24 and latitudes 6 and 9: small squares and hexagons, a few large and long thin shapes, multipolygons and one empty geometry. rcs_sim_points() and rcs_sim_lines() give points and lines in the same box.

polys <- rcs_sim_polygons(500, seed = 1)
polys

#>  7     7     0.391  b     MULTIPOLYGON (((-26.42263 8.281812, -26.41863 8.28181…

An sf object is written like a table. The dataset’s kind becomes geospatial, and its coordinate reference system (CRS) is kept in the catalog. Any CRS can be used.

store_write(st, polys, "shapes/polygons",
  title = "Polygons",
  description = "Simulated polygons in open ocean.",
  key = "id"
)
#> ℹ Writing "shapes/polygons": 500 rows in 1 file, and its index table in 1 file.
#> ✔ primary  <tempdir>/geo-store  2/2 files sent  72.8 kB  0.2s
#> ✔ MD5 identical for 2 files in 1 location. Catalogs updated.

Two files were written: the data, and an index table, explained below.

What the package adds, and why

A spatial filter on a large dataset should not read every geometry. To let the Parquet reader skip rows without looking at geometries, the package adds three columns when it writes an sf object:

  • h3: an H3 cell. H3 divides the globe into hexagonal cells at 16 resolutions; at resolution 5, the default, a cell covers about 250 km². h3 is the cell that holds the largest part of the geometry, stored as a 64-bit integer.
  • bbox: the bounding box of the geometry, four numbers (xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax).
  • .rcs_id: a row number, unique within the dataset, used to link rows to the index table. Reads drop it unless it is asked for.

Rows are sorted by h3 before they are written, so rows that lie close together sit in the same file and the same blocks of rows. A filter on h3 and bbox is a comparison of plain numbers, which the Parquet reader applies before it reads any geometry.

A geometry that crosses the edge of its cell also lies in other cells. The index table <dataset>__h3 lists every such row with every cell it touches. It is written, replaced and deleted with its dataset, and is hidden unless asked for:

print(st, index = TRUE)
#> ── rcs store ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Locations:
#>   primary  local  <tempdir>/geo-store
#> History: off (store default)
#> Datasets: 2
#>   name            kind        rows     size  files  updated
#>   shapes/
#>     polygons      geospatial   500  62.6 kB      1  2026-11-21 21:56
#>     polygons__h3  table        533  10.2 kB      1  2026-11-21 21:56

h3 and bbox come back with the data. store_h3_hex() turns the cells into the 15-character text form that other H3 tools use:

x <- store_read(st, "polygons", geometry = FALSE)
store_h3_hex(x)
#> # A tibble: 500 × 5
#>       id   area cat   h3              bbox$xmin $ymin $xmax $ymax
#>    <int>  <dbl> <chr> <chr>               <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#>  1   288 0.360  d     8556480ffffffff     -26.1  8.58 -26.1  8.58
#>  2     7 0.391  b     8556483bfffffff     -26.4  8.28 -25.9  8.54
#>  3    98 0.456  e     8556484bfffffff     -26.6  8.55 -26.6  8.55
#>  4   211 0.375  e     8556486bfffffff     -26.3  8.30 -26.3  8.31
#>  5   459 0.362  c     85564873fffffff     -26.2  8.48 -26.1  8.49
#>  6   474 0.0809 c     85564873fffffff     -26.1  8.49 -26.1  8.50
#>  7    50 0.0448 b     85564877fffffff     -26.2  8.42 -26.2  8.43
#>  8   274 0.124  a     85564877fffffff     -26.1  8.43 -26.1  8.43
#>  9   159 0.0612 e     855648b7fffffff     -25.5  8.78 -25.5  8.79
#> 10   304 0.0259 c     855648b7fffffff     -25.5  8.89 -25.5  8.89
#> # ℹ 490 more rows

Read the rows in an area

intersects keeps the rows whose geometry intersects a query shape: an sf, sfc or bbox object with a CRS.

query <- st_sfc(
  st_polygon(list(rbind(
    c(-28.5, 6.5), c(-26, 6.5), c(-27.2, 8.5), c(-28.5, 6.5)
  ))),
  crs = 4326
)
inside <- store_read(st, "polygons", intersects = query)
nrow(inside)
#> [1] 89

The read works in steps. It keeps only the files whose extent overlaps the query’s box, reads the candidate rows (those whose bbox overlaps the query’s box), and finally tests the candidates exactly with sf::st_intersects(). When the query’s box is much larger than the query (a thin diagonal strip, a line), or the query crosses the antimeridian, the H3 cells help: the read then also finds the cells the query touches, keeps only files whose range of cells matches, and keeps only rows whose h3, or a cell in the index table, is one of them. The result is the same as filtering everything in memory:

setequal(inside$id, st_filter(polys, query)$id)
#> [1] TRUE

The query may be in another CRS than the data; it is transformed first.

query_utm <- st_transform(query, 32626)
nrow(store_read(st, "polygons", intersects = query_utm))
#> [1] 89

Candidates only: exact = FALSE

The exact test needs the geometries. With exact = FALSE, or with geometry = FALSE, the read returns the candidate rows: every intersecting row and some rows that only come close. A message says so.

candidates <- store_read(st, "polygons",
  intersects = query, geometry = FALSE
)
#> ℹ Spatial filter: the geometry is not read, so the result is the candidate set.
#>   It holds every intersecting row and may hold rows that do not intersect the query.
nrow(candidates)
#> [1] 162

This is useful when the next step is a join on another column, or when an approximate answer is enough and the geometries are large.

H3 cells as query

The query can also be one or more H3 cells, of any resolution: as text, as bit64::integer64 or as an h3o H3 vector. Each stands for its cell polygon. A plain number is refused, because a double cannot hold an H3 cell exactly.

cell <- store_h3_hex(x$h3[1])
cell
#> [1] "8556480ffffffff"
store_read(st, "polygons", intersects = cell, columns = c(id, cat))
#> Simple feature collection with 1 feature and 2 fields
#> Geometry type: POLYGON
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: -26.05978 ymin: 8.578918 xmax: -26.05433 ymax: 8.584336
#> Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>      id cat                                                             geometry
#>   <int> <chr>                                                      <POLYGON [°]>
#> 1   288 d     ((-26.05978 8.578918, -26.05433 8.578918, -26.05433 8.584336, -26…

A cell finer than the stored resolution works too; a message says that the stored resolution is coarser.

fine <- h3o::h3_from_xy(7.5, -27.5, 8L)
nrow(store_read(st, "polygons", intersects = fine))
#> ℹ The query holds cells finer than the stored resolution 5; the
#> cell filter works at resolution 5.
#> [1] 1

In a lazy query

store_intersects() adds the same filter to a lazy query from store_open(), where it combines with the dplyr verbs:

store_open(st, "polygons") |>
  store_intersects(query) |>
  dplyr::filter(cat == "a") |>
  dplyr::select(id, area) |>
  dplyr::collect()
#> # A tibble: 18 × 2
#>       id   area
#>    <int>  <dbl>
#>  1   308 0.207 
#>  2   369 0.464 
#>  3   477 0.423 
#>  4   435 0.0171
#>  5   175 0.196 
#>  6   130 0.0652
#>  7   432 0.454 
#>  8   196 0.0838
#>  9    83 0.208 
#> 10    56 0.205 
#> 11    24 0.0131
#> 12   115 0.325 
#> 13   479 0.0784
#> 14   388 0.0834
#> 15   263 0.455 
#> 16   482 0.415 
#> 17   194 0.462 
#> 18   138 0.144

One file per cell: partition = "h3"

partition = "h3" writes one file per H3 parent cell. The package picks the finest resolution at which the number of files stays at most max_files and names the partition column after it (h3_p2 below: cells of resolution 2). A spatial read then opens only the files of the cells near the query. For large datasets this makes small spatial reads several times faster, most of all from a cloud bucket (see the article “Benchmark: which steps of the spatial filter pay off”).

store_write(st, polys, "shapes/polygons_by_cell",
  title = "Polygons by cell",
  description = "Simulated polygons in open ocean, one file per H3 cell.",
  key = "id",
  partition = "h3",
  max_files = 10
)
#> ℹ Writing "shapes/polygons_by_cell": 500 rows in 7 files (partition h3_p2), and its index table in 1 file.
#> ✔ primary  <tempdir>/geo-store  8/8 files sent  156.8 kB  0.2s
#> ✔ MD5 identical for 8 files in 1 location. Catalogs updated.

The work counters show which files a read opened:

small <- st_as_sfc(st_bbox(
  c(xmin = -29.5, ymin = 6.2, xmax = -29.2, ymax = 6.5),
  crs = st_crs(4326)
))
options(rcs.trace = TRUE)
near <- store_read(st, "polygons_by_cell", intersects = small)
trace <- rcs_trace()
options(rcs.trace = FALSE)
trace[trace$counter == "file_open", c("detail", "n")]
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>   detail                                                                       n
#>   <chr>                                                                    <dbl>
#> 1 shapes/polygons_by_cell/h3_p2=587654880185810943/part-c6ab2c8df9a86bde.…     1

One data file of seven was opened. The query is a compact box, so the box test alone selects the rows, and the index table is not read.

Without H3: geocode = FALSE

geocode = FALSE writes the geometries with their bbox only: no h3 column and no index table, so writing skips the geocoding. A spatial read then filters by bounding boxes alone: as fast for compact queries, slower for queries much smaller than their box, and always complete. partition = "h3" cannot be combined with it.

store_write(st, polys, "shapes/polygons_boxes",
  title = "Polygons, boxes only",
  description = "Simulated polygons in open ocean, without H3 cells.",
  key = "id",
  geocode = FALSE
)
#> ℹ Writing "shapes/polygons_boxes": 500 rows in 1 file.
#> ✔ primary  <tempdir>/geo-store  1/1 files sent  61.1 kB  0.1s
#> ✔ MD5 identical for 1 file in 1 location. Catalogs updated.
nrow(store_read(st, "polygons_boxes", intersects = query))
#> [1] 89

Rasters

A terra::SpatRaster is written as one Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF, a format that lets a reader fetch only the tiles it needs. rcs_sim_raster() returns a simulated three-layer raster over the same box.

grid <- rcs_sim_raster(seed = 1, nrow = 200, ncol = 200)
store_write(st, grid, "grids/simulated",
  title = "Simulated raster",
  description = "A simulated three-layer raster in open ocean."
)
#> ℹ Writing "grids/simulated": 40,000 cells in 1 file.
#> ✔ primary  <tempdir>/geo-store  1/1 files sent  686.5 kB  0.1s
#> ✔ MD5 identical for 1 file in 1 location. Catalogs updated.

store_read() opens the raster through GDAL. intersects crops it to the query’s bounding box, rounded outwards to whole cells.

area <- st_as_sfc(st_bbox(
  c(xmin = -28, ymin = 7, xmax = -27, ymax = 8),
  crs = st_crs(4326)
))
store_read(st, "grids/simulated", intersects = area)
#> class       : SpatRaster
#> size        : 68, 34, 3  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
#> resolution  : 0.03, 0.015  (x, y)
#> extent      : -28.02, -27, 6.99, 8.01  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
#> coord. ref. : lon/lat WGS 84 (EPSG:4326)
#> source(s)   : memory
#> varname     : part-a2f2827357463723
#> names       :      height, cover, moisture
#> min values  : -101.836024,     1,   0.0011
#> max values  :  103.103297,     5,   0.9989

A raster has one file: it cannot be partitioned or updated, only replaced. Filters, columns, geometry and exact do not apply to rasters, and store_open() and store_sample() refuse them.

Shapes across the antimeridian or around a pole

Geometries that cross the antimeridian (longitude ±180°) or contain a pole are stored and found correctly. The package detects them, finds their cells on the sphere, and always lists them in the index table, because their bounding box, which may span all longitudes, says little about where they lie. Query shapes of this kind are handled the same way. These rows are defined on the sphere: with sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE) a read is not guaranteed to find them. rcs_sim_polygons(special = TRUE) adds one such polygon of each kind, for trying this out.
